title: Why braking at the speed camera doesn't save you
description:
Average speed cameras never measure your speed. They read your number plate at two points and divide: 5 km in 150 seconds is 120 km/h, however slowly you passed each camera. And if you passed both at 95, the mean value theorem says your speedometer still read exactly 120 at some moment in between, because a speed that averages 120 has to pass through 120. At 100 km/h the same 5 km take 3 minutes, so braking for the cameras bought you a fine to save 30 seconds. Average speed cameras (SPECS in the UK, section control in Austria, Tutor in Italy) have done this division since 1999.

Numbers checked in code: every figure computed, plus 100,000 random speed profiles that read 95 at both cameras and average 120 (every one went above 120 and passed through exactly 120). Sources: Wikipedia, SPECS (speed camera), Traffic enforcement camera, Mean value theorem.

facts_checked: 5 km in 150 s = 120 km/h; at 100 km/h 5 km take 180 s = 3 minutes, 30 s saved; CTA 10 km in 5 minutes = 120 km/h (verify.py)

Mean value theorem: a speed profile reading 95 at both ends and averaging 120 goes above 120 and passes through exactly 120 (100,000 random smooth profiles, all did; 100,000 random trips all hit their own average speed at some moment) (verify.py)
Mean value theorem driving example: at some moment during the trip 'its instantaneous speed equals its average speed for the whole trip' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_value_theorem)
Average speed cameras time a vehicle between two sites a known distance apart and compute the average speed (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_enforcement_camera)

SPECS reads the number plate at each site with ANPR and computes average speed from distance and time; UK Home Office type approved in 1999; similar systems: Netherlands trajectcontrole, Austria Section Control, Italy Tutor (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SPECS_(speed_camera))

beats.say: You braked for the camera. You still got fined.
It never clocked your speed. It clocked your time.
Two cameras, 5 kilometers apart. The limit is 100.
Camera one reads your plate. Camera two reads it 150 seconds later.
5 kilometers in 150 seconds is 120 kilometers an hour. Over the limit.
But you braked to 95 at both cameras. So how can they fine a speed nobody saw?
Draw your speed: 95 at the start, 95 at the end. To average 120, it has to climb above 120.
Your speed can't jump. So on the way up, it passes 120 exactly. At that moment, you were doing 120.
At 100, those 5 kilometers take 3 minutes. You saved 30 seconds.
Your speedometer always hits your average at least once. That's the mean value theorem. The camera never needed to see you.
